questiontext.text: Black-box testing designs its tests based on:

answer.text: The specification and external behavior, without knowledge of the internal code structure

feedback.text: Correct — black-box (specification-based) testing treats the implementation as opaque.

answer.text: The internal control-flow graph of the code

feedback.text: That is white-box (structural) testing, which uses the code's structure.

answer.text: The number of source lines executed by the tests

feedback.text: That describes a coverage measurement, not the black-box design basis.

answer.text: The compiler's optimization settings

feedback.text: Compiler settings are unrelated to how black-box tests are derived.

generalfeedback.text: Black-box (specification-based) testing derives tests from requirements and external behavior, treating the implementation as opaque — no code knowledge is used.

questiontext.text: White-box (structural) testing designs its tests based on:

answer.text: Knowledge of the internal code structure, such as statements, branches, and paths

feedback.text: Correct — white-box (glass-box) testing uses the internal structure of the code.

answer.text: Only the published requirements, ignoring the code entirely

feedback.text: That is black-box testing; white-box uses the code structure.

answer.text: The user's subjective satisfaction with the product

feedback.text: That is closer to validation/usability, not structural testing.

answer.text: The hardware the program will run on

feedback.text: The target hardware is not the basis of white-box test design.

generalfeedback.text: White-box (structural / glass-box) testing uses the internal structure of the code — statements, branches, paths, conditions — to derive and measure tests.

questiontext.text: Grey-box testing is characterized by:

answer.text: Partial knowledge of the internal structure combined with tests driven through external interfaces

feedback.text: Correct — grey-box uses some internal insight (e.g. architecture or DB schema) while testing externally.

answer.text: Complete ignorance of both the specification and the code

feedback.text: A tester always uses some basis; grey-box specifically uses partial internal knowledge.

answer.text: A full mathematical proof of correctness

feedback.text: That is formal verification, not grey-box testing.

answer.text: Testing only the colors of the graphical user interface

feedback.text: Grey-box is about the level of internal knowledge, not UI appearance.

generalfeedback.text: Grey-box testing uses partial internal knowledge (architecture, data schema, key algorithms) to design tests that are still exercised through external interfaces.

questiontext.text: Static testing is best described as:

answer.text: Examining the software artifacts (documents or code) without executing the program

feedback.text: Correct — static techniques find defects by examination, with no execution.

answer.text: Running the program with many different inputs

feedback.text: That is dynamic testing, which requires execution.

answer.text: Measuring response time under heavy load

feedback.text: That is a dynamic, non-functional activity (performance testing).

answer.text: Deploying to production and monitoring live users

feedback.text: Monitoring a running system is dynamic, not static.

generalfeedback.text: Static testing (reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, static analysis) finds defects by examining artifacts without executing the program.

questiontext.text: Dynamic testing is best described as:

answer.text: Executing the program with inputs and observing its behavior

feedback.text: Correct — dynamic testing runs the software and compares behavior to expectations.

answer.text: Reading the code together in a review meeting

feedback.text: That is a static technique (review); nothing is executed.

answer.text: Checking a requirements document for typographical errors

feedback.text: That is static examination of a document, not dynamic testing.

answer.text: Analyzing the source with a tool but never running it

feedback.text: That is static analysis; dynamic testing requires execution.

generalfeedback.text: Dynamic testing requires executing the software and comparing the observed behavior against expected results.

questiontext.text: Functional testing is primarily concerned with:

answer.text: What the system does — whether it produces the correct outputs for given inputs

feedback.text: Correct — functional testing checks behavior against the specified functions.

answer.text: How fast the system responds under load

feedback.text: That is a non-functional (performance) concern.

answer.text: How resistant the system is to attackers

feedback.text: That is a non-functional (security) concern.

answer.text: How maintainable the source code is

feedback.text: Maintainability is a non-functional quality attribute, not a function.

generalfeedback.text: Functional testing checks the functions/behavior of the system against the requirements — what it does — rather than how well it does it.

questiontext.text: Non-functional testing primarily evaluates:

answer.text: Quality attributes such as performance, security, usability, and reliability

feedback.text: Correct — non-functional testing targets how well the system operates.

answer.text: Whether each required feature returns the correct result

feedback.text: That is functional testing (what the system does).

answer.text: Whether every statement in the code is executed

feedback.text: That is a structural coverage (white-box) concern.

answer.text: Whether the requirements document is grammatically complete

feedback.text: That is a static review concern, not non-functional testing.

generalfeedback.text: Non-functional testing targets how well the system operates — performance, security, usability, reliability, portability, etc. — rather than which features work.

questiontext.text: In the classic V&V distinction, verification asks:

answer.text: "Are we building the product right?" — does it conform to its specification?

feedback.text: Correct — verification checks conformance to the spec and standards at each stage.

answer.text: "Are we building the right product?" — does it meet the users' needs?

feedback.text: That is validation, not verification.

answer.text: "Is the product faster than the competitors' products?"

feedback.text: That is a benchmarking/performance question, not verification.

answer.text: "Will customers be willing to pay for the product?"

feedback.text: That is a market question, unrelated to the V&V distinction.

generalfeedback.text: Verification checks conformance to specifications, designs and standards at each development stage — "building the product right."

questiontext.text: In the classic V&V distinction, validation asks:

answer.text: "Are we building the right product?" — does it meet the users' actual needs?

feedback.text: Correct — validation checks fitness for use against real user needs.

answer.text: "Are we building the product right?" — does it conform to the spec?

feedback.text: That is verification, not validation.

answer.text: "Does the source code compile without warnings?"

feedback.text: That is a static/build concern, not validation.

answer.text: "Is every branch in the code covered by a test?"

feedback.text: That is a white-box coverage concern, not validation.

generalfeedback.text: Validation checks fitness for use — whether the finished product satisfies the users' real needs — "building the right product."

questiontext.text: Boundary value analysis is an example of which kind of technique?

answer.text: Black-box — it uses the input specification and partitions, not the code

feedback.text: Correct — BVA derives tests from the boundaries of specified input partitions.

answer.text: White-box — it requires the control-flow graph

feedback.text: BVA needs no code structure; it works from the input spec.

answer.text: Static — it never executes the program

feedback.text: BVA cases are executed against the program, so it is dynamic, not static.

answer.text: Non-functional — it measures performance

feedback.text: BVA checks functional behavior at input boundaries, not performance.

generalfeedback.text: Boundary value analysis derives tests from the boundaries of input partitions in the specification, with no code knowledge — a black-box technique.

questiontext.text: Branch (decision) coverage is which kind of technique?

answer.text: White-box — it is defined over the code's decisions and branches

feedback.text: Correct — branch coverage is measured against the code's structure.

answer.text: Black-box — it needs only the specification

feedback.text: Branch coverage requires knowledge of the code's branches, so it is white-box.

answer.text: Non-functional — it measures usability

feedback.text: Branch coverage is a structural metric, not a quality attribute.

answer.text: Static — it needs no execution

feedback.text: Measuring branch coverage requires executing the tests, so it is dynamic.

generalfeedback.text: Branch coverage is measured over the code's branches, requiring knowledge of internal structure — a white-box technique. (Measuring it also requires execution, so it is dynamic.)

questiontext.text: A code review (inspection) is a form of static testing.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a review examines the code without executing it, so it is static.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Reviews find defects by reading, not running, the code — they are static.

generalfeedback.text: Reviews, walkthroughs and inspections are static techniques: defects are found by examination, without executing the program.

questiontext.text: Equivalence partitioning is which kind of technique?

answer.text: Black-box — it partitions the input domain from the specification

feedback.text: Correct — equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes from the spec.

answer.text: White-box — it partitions the code paths

feedback.text: Equivalence partitioning works on the input domain, not code paths.

answer.text: Static — it needs no test execution

feedback.text: The resulting cases are executed, so it is a dynamic, black-box technique.

answer.text: A verification-only activity that never runs the software

feedback.text: Its test cases are executed against the software, so this is wrong.

generalfeedback.text: Equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes derived from the specification, without code knowledge — a black-box technique.

questiontext.text: Statement coverage is which kind of technique?

answer.text: White-box — it is defined over the code's executable statements

feedback.text: Correct — statement coverage is measured against the code's structure.

answer.text: Black-box — it needs only the requirements

feedback.text: Statement coverage requires knowledge of the code, so it is white-box.

answer.text: Non-functional — it measures reliability

feedback.text: Statement coverage is a structural metric, not a quality attribute.

answer.text: Static — no execution is required

feedback.text: Measuring statement coverage requires running the tests, so it is dynamic.

generalfeedback.text: Statement coverage is measured over the executable statements of the code, so it is a white-box (structural) technique; measuring it is dynamic (requires execution).

questiontext.text: Black-box testing requires access to the program's source code.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — black-box testing is based on the specification and behavior, not the source.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Black-box treats the implementation as opaque; it does not need the source (that is white-box).

generalfeedback.text: Black-box testing derives tests from the specification and external behavior; the source code is not required. Needing the source is the mark of white-box testing.

questiontext.text: A tester drives a web application through its public UI but uses knowledge of the database schema to craft inputs and check the stored results. This is best classified as:

answer.text: Grey-box testing

feedback.text: Correct — partial internal knowledge (the schema) used while driving the system externally is grey-box.

answer.text: Pure black-box testing

feedback.text: Pure black-box uses no internal knowledge; here the schema is used, so it is grey-box.

answer.text: Pure white-box testing

feedback.text: White-box would drive tests from the code structure; here tests run through the UI with only partial knowledge.

answer.text: Static analysis

feedback.text: The system is executed through the UI, so this is dynamic, not static.

generalfeedback.text: Using partial internal knowledge (the DB schema) while exercising the system through external interfaces is the defining pattern of grey-box testing.

questiontext.text: A specification walkthrough is a dynamic testing activity.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — a walkthrough examines a document without executing software, so it is static.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Walkthroughs, like reviews and inspections, are static — no program is executed.

generalfeedback.text: Walkthroughs (like reviews and inspections) are static techniques — defects are found by examination, with no code executed.

questiontext.text: Performance testing (measuring throughput and response time under load) is classified as:

answer.text: Non-functional testing

feedback.text: Correct — performance is a quality attribute (how well), so it is non-functional.

answer.text: Functional testing

feedback.text: Functional testing checks what the system does; performance is about how well it does it.

answer.text: White-box testing

feedback.text: Performance testing is usually black-box; the black/white axis is separate from functional/non-functional anyway.

answer.text: Static testing

feedback.text: Performance testing executes the system under load, so it is dynamic, not static.

generalfeedback.text: Performance concerns a quality attribute (how well the system performs, not which features work), so it is non-functional. It is also dynamic and usually black-box.

questiontext.text: Reviewing the requirements specification against the applicable standards and the customer contract is an example of:

answer.text: Verification — conformance to the specification and process ("building the product right")

feedback.text: Correct — a requirements review checks conformance to standards and the spec.

answer.text: Validation — fitness for the users' real needs

feedback.text: Validation confirms real-world fitness of the delivered product, typically dynamically; a spec review is verification.

answer.text: Non-functional testing

feedback.text: A document review is a static verification activity, not a non-functional test.

answer.text: Dynamic testing

feedback.text: A review executes nothing, so it is static, not dynamic.

generalfeedback.text: A requirements review checks conformance to specifications and standards — a verification activity, and a static one.

questiontext.text: User Acceptance Testing (UAT), in which real users try the delivered system to confirm it meets their needs, is an example of:

answer.text: Validation — fitness for use ("building the right product")

feedback.text: Correct — UAT confirms the product satisfies actual user needs.

answer.text: Verification — conformance to the design document

feedback.text: Conformance to the design is verification; UAT checks real user needs, which is validation.

answer.text: Static testing

feedback.text: UAT runs the delivered system, so it is dynamic, not static.

answer.text: White-box testing

feedback.text: Users exercise the system through its interfaces, not its code — it is black-box, and the question is really about V&V.

generalfeedback.text: UAT confirms the product satisfies the users' actual needs — validation. It is also dynamic and black-box.

name.text: Which axis: BVA vs branch coverage

questiontext.text: Boundary value analysis and branch coverage differ primarily along which classification axis?

answer.text: Black-box vs white-box (knowledge of the internal code structure)

feedback.text: Correct — BVA is spec-based (black-box) while branch coverage is structure-based (white-box).

answer.text: Static vs dynamic

feedback.text: Both are dynamic (their tests are executed); they do not differ on this axis.

answer.text: Functional vs non-functional

feedback.text: Both are oriented to functional correctness; the real difference is the knowledge basis.

answer.text: Verification vs validation

feedback.text: Both are typically verification-oriented; they differ on black-box vs white-box.

generalfeedback.text: BVA is black-box (derived from the spec) and branch coverage is white-box (derived from the code structure); they differ on the knowledge/structure axis. Both are dynamic.

questiontext.text: A black-box acceptance suite is rewritten to run automatically via a UI-driving tool. On the black-box/white-box axis, the automated suite is now:

answer.text: Still black-box — automation is an orthogonal axis and adds no code-structure knowledge

feedback.text: Correct — manual vs automated is independent of black-box vs white-box.

answer.text: Now white-box, because a tool interacts with the program

feedback.text: Automating a test does not give it knowledge of the code's internal structure.

answer.text: Now grey-box, because automation tools always read the source

feedback.text: A UI-driving tool does not read the source; the knowledge basis is unchanged.

answer.text: Neither black- nor white-box any more

feedback.text: It remains black-box; only the manual/automated axis changed.

generalfeedback.text: Manual vs automated is orthogonal to black-box vs white-box. Automating a black-box suite keeps it black-box; the knowledge basis is unchanged.

questiontext.text: A tool scans the source code for null-pointer risks and unused variables without ever running the program. This activity is:

answer.text: Static analysis — a static technique that examines code without executing it

feedback.text: Correct — no execution takes place, so it is static analysis.

answer.text: Dynamic testing — it executes the program

feedback.text: The tool never runs the program, so it is static, not dynamic.

answer.text: Black-box testing — it ignores the code

feedback.text: It reads the source (structure), so it is not black-box.

answer.text: Performance testing

feedback.text: It analyzes code, not runtime performance.

generalfeedback.text: Static analysis examines the source/structure without execution, so it is static. Because it uses the code structure, it is structure-based rather than spec-based.

name.text: Family of error guessing and exploratory

questiontext.text: Error guessing and exploratory testing, which rely on the tester's experience rather than a formal model, belong to which family?

answer.text: Experience-based techniques

feedback.text: Correct — these are experience-based techniques driven by tester intuition and skill.

answer.text: Structure-based (white-box) coverage techniques

feedback.text: They do not use code structure or coverage criteria.

answer.text: Static review techniques

feedback.text: They execute the software, so they are dynamic, not static reviews.

answer.text: Non-functional techniques

feedback.text: They target functional defects using experience, not quality attributes.

generalfeedback.text: Error guessing and exploratory testing are experience-based techniques — a dynamic, black-box family driven by the tester's knowledge and intuition rather than a formal specification or the code structure.

questiontext.text: State-transition testing derives its test cases from a behavioral state model built from the requirements. It is a:

answer.text: Black-box technique — derived from a spec/behavioral model, not the code

feedback.text: Correct — the state model comes from the requirements, so it is black-box.

answer.text: White-box technique — derived from the control-flow graph

feedback.text: The model is behavioral (from the spec), not the code's control-flow graph.

answer.text: Static technique — no execution

feedback.text: The resulting cases are executed against the system, so it is dynamic.

answer.text: Non-functional technique

feedback.text: It checks functional behavior via states and transitions, not a quality attribute.

generalfeedback.text: State-transition testing uses a behavioral model derived from the specification, treating the implementation as opaque — a black-box technique.

questiontext.text: Stress testing (pushing the system beyond normal load to see how it degrades or fails) is:

answer.text: Non-functional (and dynamic) testing

feedback.text: Correct — it evaluates behavior under extreme load, a quality attribute, by executing the system.

answer.text: Functional testing

feedback.text: It checks a quality attribute under load, not whether specific features return correct results.

answer.text: Static testing

feedback.text: It runs the system under load, so it is dynamic, not static.

answer.text: White-box coverage measurement

feedback.text: It measures behavior under load, not code structure coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Stress/load testing evaluates a quality attribute (behavior under extreme load), so it is non-functional; because it executes the system it is also dynamic.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a verification activity rather than a validation activity?

answer.text: Inspecting a module's code against its detailed design document

feedback.text: Correct — checking conformance to the design is verification.

answer.text: Having end users trial the product to confirm it meets their needs

feedback.text: That confirms fitness for use — validation.

answer.text: Running a beta program to gather real-world feedback

feedback.text: A beta program checks real user needs — validation.

answer.text: Confirming the finished system solves the customer's actual problem

feedback.text: That is fitness for use — validation.

generalfeedback.text: Checking a module against its design document is verification (conformance to spec). The other options confirm fitness for the users' real needs — validation.

questiontext.text: Security testing (checking resistance to unauthorized access) is primarily:

answer.text: Non-functional testing

feedback.text: Correct — security is a quality attribute, so security testing is non-functional.

answer.text: Functional testing

feedback.text: Security concerns a quality attribute (how well it resists attack), not a listed feature's output.

answer.text: A purely static technique

feedback.text: Security testing typically executes the system (e.g. penetration tests), so it is dynamic.

answer.text: A verification-only activity

feedback.text: Security testing is a non-functional test category, not a V&V stage label.

generalfeedback.text: Security is a quality attribute, so security testing is non-functional. It is typically dynamic and may be grey- or black-box depending on the knowledge used.

name.text: Clearest axis: walkthrough vs load test

questiontext.text: The clearest classification difference between a walkthrough and a load test is:

answer.text: Static vs dynamic — a walkthrough executes nothing, a load test executes the system

feedback.text: Correct — the defining contrast is execution.

answer.text: Black-box vs white-box

feedback.text: A walkthrough is not really placed on the black/white-box axis; the definitional contrast here is static vs dynamic.

answer.text: Verification vs validation

feedback.text: Both can serve verification; the clear contrast is that one executes and the other does not.

answer.text: Manual vs automated

feedback.text: Either could be manual or automated; the defining difference is execution.

generalfeedback.text: A walkthrough is static (nothing is executed) while a load test is dynamic (the system runs under load); the static-vs-dynamic axis is the defining contrast.

questiontext.text: Basis-path testing (deriving tests from the code's linearly independent paths) is a:

answer.text: White-box (structure-based) technique

feedback.text: Correct — basis-path testing is derived from the code's control-flow graph.

answer.text: Black-box technique

feedback.text: It uses the code's paths, so it is structure-based, not spec-based.

answer.text: Non-functional technique

feedback.text: It targets structural coverage of paths, not a quality attribute.

answer.text: Static technique

feedback.text: Its tests are executed, so it is dynamic, not static.

generalfeedback.text: Basis-path testing is derived from the control-flow graph (independent paths) of the code, so it is white-box / structure-based, and dynamic.

questiontext.text: Load testing executes the running system, is driven purely through external interfaces with no code knowledge, and measures response time under heavy traffic. Across the three axes it is:

answer.text: Dynamic, black-box, and non-functional

feedback.text: Correct — it executes (dynamic), uses no code knowledge (black-box), and measures a quality attribute (non-functional).

answer.text: Static, white-box, and functional

feedback.text: It executes the system and uses no code knowledge, so it is dynamic and black-box, and it targets performance (non-functional).

answer.text: Dynamic, white-box, and non-functional

feedback.text: It uses no knowledge of the code's internal structure, so it is black-box, not white-box.

answer.text: Static, black-box, and functional

feedback.text: It runs the system (dynamic) and measures performance (non-functional).

generalfeedback.text: Load testing executes the system (dynamic), needs no internal code knowledge (black-box), and targets a performance quality attribute (non-functional).

questiontext.text: Because static analysis inspects the source code, it is a form of dynamic white-box testing.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — static analysis is structure-based but does NOT execute the program, so it is static, not dynamic.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Static analysis uses the code structure but performs no execution, so it cannot be dynamic testing.

generalfeedback.text: Static analysis is structure-based (it uses the code) yet static (no execution). "White-box" refers to knowledge of the structure, not to execution — so "uses the code" does not make it dynamic.

name.text: Why grey-box is not black plus white

questiontext.text: Which statement best captures why grey-box testing is not simply "black-box plus white-box"?

answer.text: It uses partial internal knowledge to design better externally-driven tests, rather than performing the complete sets of both black-box and white-box tests

feedback.text: Correct — grey-box combines a limited source of internal insight with external testing; it is not the union of the two full test sets.

answer.text: It performs every possible black-box test and every possible white-box test

feedback.text: Grey-box uses only partial internal knowledge; it does not run the full white-box test set.

answer.text: It is identical to white-box testing but with a different name

feedback.text: Grey-box uses only partial internal knowledge and drives tests externally, unlike full white-box testing.

answer.text: It requires no knowledge of either the specification or the code

feedback.text: That would be neither; grey-box specifically uses partial internal knowledge.

generalfeedback.text: Grey-box combines sources of knowledge — using limited internal insight (architecture, schema, key algorithms) to target external tests. It is not the union of complete black-box and white-box test sets.

questiontext.text: MC/DC (Modified Condition/Decision Coverage) is best classified as:

answer.text: White-box and dynamic — defined over code conditions and measured by executing tests

feedback.text: Correct — it is a structural criterion whose satisfaction is observed only by running the tests.

answer.text: White-box and static — coverage can be computed without running the program

feedback.text: MC/DC is structural, but coverage is only observed by executing the tests, so it is dynamic.

answer.text: Black-box and dynamic

feedback.text: MC/DC is defined over the code's conditions, so it is white-box, not black-box.

answer.text: Black-box and static

feedback.text: It is defined over code conditions (white-box) and requires execution (dynamic).

generalfeedback.text: MC/DC is a structural (white-box) criterion, but coverage is only observed by executing the tests, so it is dynamic. Structural coverage criteria are not static.

questiontext.text: Executing a module's unit tests derived from its detailed design specification, to confirm the module conforms to that design, is chiefly an act of:

answer.text: Verification — conformance to the specification

feedback.text: Correct — confirming conformance to the design spec is verification.

answer.text: Validation — fitness for the end user's real needs

feedback.text: Validation checks real user needs; here we check conformance to the design — verification.

answer.text: Non-functional testing

feedback.text: It checks functional conformance to the design, not a quality attribute.

answer.text: Static analysis

feedback.text: The tests are executed, so this is dynamic, and its V&V role is verification.

generalfeedback.text: Confirming conformance to the design specification is verification. The unit testing here is dynamic (and could be white-box), but on the V&V axis its role is verification.

name.text: Spec satisfied but wrong for users

questiontext.text: A system perfectly satisfies its written requirements, yet those requirements misunderstood what users actually needed. Which activity is designed to catch this?

answer.text: Validation — it checks fitness for real user needs, independent of the written spec

feedback.text: Correct — validation catches "building the wrong product" even when the spec is met.

answer.text: Verification — it checks conformance to the written spec

feedback.text: Verification would pass here, because the product matches the (flawed) spec.

answer.text: Statement coverage

feedback.text: Coverage measures which code ran, not whether the requirements were right.

answer.text: Static analysis of the source

feedback.text: Static analysis inspects code quality, not whether the requirements meet user needs.

generalfeedback.text: Verification would pass (the product matches the spec), but the spec itself is wrong. Only validation, which checks against real user needs, catches "building the wrong product."

name.text: Why BVA is in the black-box family

questiontext.text: Boundary value analysis is classified in the black-box family because:

answer.text: Its cases are derived from the boundaries of input partitions in the specification, needing no knowledge of the code

feedback.text: Correct — the test basis is the specified input domain, not the code.

answer.text: It measures which branches of the code were executed

feedback.text: That describes branch coverage, a white-box technique, not BVA.

answer.text: It never executes the program under test

feedback.text: BVA cases are executed; the reason it is black-box is its spec-based test basis, not a lack of execution.

answer.text: It only evaluates non-functional quality attributes

feedback.text: BVA targets functional behavior at input boundaries, not quality attributes.

generalfeedback.text: BVA belongs to the black-box family because its cases come from the boundaries of the specified input domain, requiring no knowledge of the code's internal structure.

questiontext.text: Reporting 90% branch coverage demonstrates that thorough black-box testing was performed.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — branch coverage is a white-box (structural) measure and says nothing about specification-based black-box testing.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Coverage is a structural metric; a high value does not indicate the specification was tested (black-box).

generalfeedback.text: Coverage metrics are white-box / structural. High coverage does not imply the specification was tested (black-box), and vice versa; the black/white-box and coverage notions are independent.

questiontext.text: Which technique is both white-box (structure-based) AND static (no execution)?

answer.text: Data-flow static analysis of the source code

feedback.text: Correct — it uses the code structure (white-box) but never executes it (static).

answer.text: Branch coverage measurement

feedback.text: Branch coverage is white-box but dynamic — it requires executing the tests.

answer.text: Boundary value analysis

feedback.text: BVA is black-box (spec-based) and dynamic.

answer.text: Load testing

feedback.text: Load testing is black-box and dynamic.

generalfeedback.text: Data-flow static analysis examines the code's structure (white-box) without executing it (static). Branch coverage is white-box but dynamic; BVA is black-box; load testing is black-box and dynamic.

questiontext.text: A developer writes unit tests from the code, runs them, and asserts each function returns the correct result. Ignoring any coverage measurement, across the three axes these tests are:

answer.text: White-box, dynamic, and functional

feedback.text: Correct — derived from the code (white-box), executed (dynamic), and checking correct outputs (functional).

answer.text: Black-box, static, and non-functional

feedback.text: They are derived from the code (white-box), executed (dynamic), and check correct results (functional).

answer.text: White-box, static, and non-functional

feedback.text: Running the tests makes them dynamic, and checking correct results makes them functional.

answer.text: Black-box, dynamic, and functional

feedback.text: Because they are written from the code, they are white-box, not black-box.

generalfeedback.text: Tests derived from the code are white-box; running them is dynamic; asserting that each function returns the correct result is functional. Design basis, execution, and functional/non-functional are three separate axes.

questiontext.text: A penetration tester is given partial architecture diagrams and some API internals, then attacks the running system to find security flaws. This is best described as:

answer.text: Grey-box, dynamic, and non-functional

feedback.text: Correct — partial internal knowledge (grey-box), attacking a running system (dynamic), targeting security (non-functional).

answer.text: Black-box, static, and functional

feedback.text: The tester has partial internal knowledge (grey-box) and executes the system (dynamic), targeting a quality attribute (non-functional).

answer.text: White-box, static, and functional

feedback.text: Only partial knowledge is used (grey-box), the system is executed (dynamic), and the goal is security (non-functional).

answer.text: Pure black-box and functional

feedback.text: Using partial internals makes it grey-box, and the security goal is non-functional.

generalfeedback.text: Partial internal knowledge makes it grey-box; attacking the running system makes it dynamic; targeting security (a quality attribute) makes it non-functional.

questiontext.text: On the V&V axis and the static/dynamic axis, a formal inspection of a design document is:

answer.text: Verification and static

feedback.text: Correct — it checks conformance to the spec/standards (verification) and executes nothing (static).

answer.text: Validation and dynamic

feedback.text: An inspection executes nothing (static) and checks conformance to spec (verification).

answer.text: Verification and dynamic

feedback.text: It is verification, but nothing is executed, so it is static, not dynamic.

answer.text: Validation and static

feedback.text: It is static, but it checks conformance to spec, so it is verification, not validation.

generalfeedback.text: A design inspection checks conformance to the specification and standards (verification) and executes nothing (static).

name.text: Regression testing is white-box by definition?

questiontext.text: Regression testing is, by definition, a white-box technique.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — regression testing is defined by its purpose (re-testing after a change) and can be black-box or white-box, manual or automated.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Regression is about when and why you test, not the knowledge basis; it can be either black- or white-box.

generalfeedback.text: Regression testing is categorized by purpose — confirming that a change did not break existing behavior — an axis orthogonal to black-box vs white-box. A regression suite may be either.

questiontext.text: Which statement about verification and validation is correct?

answer.text: Verification can be static (e.g. reviews) or dynamic (e.g. unit tests against the spec), while validation is normally dynamic

feedback.text: Correct — verification spans both static and dynamic methods; validation is usually dynamic.

answer.text: Verification is always static and validation is always dynamic

feedback.text: Verification also includes dynamic methods, such as unit/integration tests checking conformance to the spec.

answer.text: Verification and validation are the same activity under two names

feedback.text: They are distinct: conformance to spec versus fitness for user needs.

answer.text: Validation must always be completed before any verification

feedback.text: There is no such strict ordering; verification runs throughout development.

generalfeedback.text: Verification spans both static (reviews, inspections) and dynamic (spec-based unit/integration tests) methods; validation — confirming real-world fitness — is typically dynamic. They are distinct activities and not strictly ordered validation-first.

name.text: EP design vs execution on two axes

questiontext.text: A tester designs cases with equivalence partitioning (from the spec) and then runs them against the program. On the knowledge axis and the static/dynamic axis respectively, this is:

answer.text: Black-box and dynamic — the design is spec-based, but running the cases executes the program

feedback.text: Correct — the design technique is black-box; executing the cases is dynamic.

answer.text: White-box and static

feedback.text: The design uses the spec (black-box), and running the cases makes it dynamic.

answer.text: Black-box and static

feedback.text: The cases are executed against the program, so the activity is dynamic, not static.

answer.text: White-box and dynamic

feedback.text: Equivalence partitioning is spec-based, so it is black-box, not white-box.

generalfeedback.text: Equivalence partitioning is a black-box design technique (spec-based); executing the resulting cases is dynamic. The design basis and the execution mode are separate axes.
